lesson.title: Where Revenue Meets Cost: Marginal Profit
lesson.summary: Profit is revenue minus cost, so marginal profit is marginal revenue minus marginal cost, and the most profitable production level sits right where the two are equal.
lesson.body:
Profit is simply what is left of revenue after cost is paid: P(x) = R(x) - C(x). Differentiating both sides, using the fact that the derivative of a difference is the difference of derivatives, gives marginal profit directly in terms of the two quantities from the previous chapters: P'(x) = R'(x) - C'(x) = MR(x) - MC(x). Marginal profit is not a new idea to compute from scratch; it is marginal revenue minus marginal cost, built entirely from pieces already in hand.

That relationship doubles as a decision rule. If MR(x) is greater than MC(x), marginal profit is positive, and producing one more unit adds more revenue than it costs, worth doing. If MR(x) is less than MC(x), marginal profit is negative, and the next unit actually loses money. The most profitable production level tends to sit right where MR(x) equals MC(x), the point where marginal profit crosses zero, a connection that becomes central once optimization enters the picture.

Combine the cost function from the marginal cost chapter, C(x) = 0.5x^2 + 20x + 200, with the revenue function from the marginal revenue chapter, R(x) = 100x - 0.5x^2. Profit is P(x) = R(x) - C(x) = (100x - 0.5x^2) - (0.5x^2 + 20x + 200) = -x^2 + 80x - 200, so P'(x) = -2x + 80. As a check, MR(x) - MC(x) = (100 - x) - (x + 20) = 80 - 2x, which matches P'(x) exactly, confirming the difference rule did its job. At x = 30, P'(30) = 80 - 60 = 20 dollars; using the individual pieces, MR(30) = 70 and MC(30) = 30 + 20 = 50, and 70 - 50 = 20, the same answer both ways. Checking against the actual profit: P(30) = -900 + 2400 - 200 = 1300 dollars, and P(31) = -961 + 2480 - 200 = 1319 dollars, an actual gain of 19 dollars, close to the $20 marginal estimate.

Since MR(30) = 70 exceeds MC(30) = 50, marginal profit is positive at x = 30, so producing the 31st unit is worthwhile, and a business following this rule would keep expanding production as long as marginal revenue stays above marginal cost.
